newsitem.title: USA: Ugandan fossils may be oldest ape ancestors - study.
newsitem.headline: Ugandan fossils may be oldest ape ancestors - study.

text.p: A set of Ugandan fossils, some discovered more than 30 years ago, may be the oldest known ancestors of humans and apes, anthropologists reported on Thursday.

In the early 1960s, anthropologists discovered facial, dental and vertebrae remains from two sites in Uganda, dating from the Miocene period 10 to 25 million years ago. But researchers were not quite sure how to interpret or classify those findings.
Then in 1994-95, a research team returned to the site and found more fossils that appeared to belong to the same large-bodied hominoid or human-like animal.

In a report in this week's edition of the journal Science, they argue that the finds date to at least 20.6 million years ago and are the "earliest evidence for a significantly ape-like body plan in the primate fossil record."

The conclusions have not been immediately accepted by everyone in the field, which was also absorbing other startling findings about other ancient apes. But the Ugandan find was likely to stir new theories and research about the evolution of apes and the rise of the human.

"I think we can expect continuing clouds of discomfort as to how to handle all this new material," University of Toronto paleoanthropologist David Begun told Science. "But it's the beginning of a great research enterprise."

The team, including Northern Illinois University anthropologist Daniel Gebo and Laura MacClatchy of Stony Brook, have named the Ugandan tree-dweller as Morotopithecus bishopi, a name derived from the site Moroto and the 1960s researcher W. Bishop who first discovered them.
The vertebrae found in the 1960s suggests that the ape had a stiff back, which suggests the upright posture of modern apes. But the teeth and face bones were much more primitive.

When the other bones were found in the 1990s, a partial shoulder and two leg bones seemed less primitive. The round shoulder socket suggested an advanced mobility and the leg bone, or femur, also seemed to share traits with modern primates, key findings in how Gebo and his team classified them.
